n.text: N=326 (ITT); CR/CRi analyzed in the first 218 patients enrolled (ITT218)

citations.quote: B1931022 (N=326)	Pivotal Phase 3 trial

In the analysis of the primary endpoint of complete response or complete response with incomplete hematological recovery (CR/CRI) in the first 218 patients enrolled who received inotuzumab ozogamicin, the CR/CRI rate was 81% (95% CI: 72%, 88%) compared to 29% (95% CI: 21%, 39%) for the patients who received a investigator's choice of chemotherapy.

result.text: CR/CRi rate 81% (95% CI 72%, 88%) vs 29% (95% CI 21%, 39%) for chemotherapy in ITT218. OS in ITT (N=326) did not reach statistical significance: HR 0.770 (97.5% CI 0.578, 1.026); median OS 7.7 months vs 6.7 months, exceeding the prespecified 1-sided p-value boundary of 0.0104.

citations.quote: In the analysis of the primary endpoint of complete response or complete response with incomplete hematological recovery (CR/CRI) in the first 218 patients enrolled who received inotuzumab ozogamicin, the CR/CRI rate was 81% (95% CI: 72%, 88%) compared to 29% (95% CI: 21%, 39%) for the patients who received a investigator's choice of chemotherapy.

An improvement in overall survival for the full ITT population (N=326) did not reach statistical significance in the pivotal phase 3 study (B1931022) as it exceeded the prespecified 1-sided p-value boundary of 0.0104. The estimated hazard ratio (primary analysis cutoff date of 8 March 2016) for the primary endpoint of overall survival (OS) in the ITT population was 0.770 (97.5% CI: 0.578, 1.026) with an estimated median OS of 7.7 months (95% CI 6, 9.2) for inotuzumab ozogamicin versus 6.7 months (95% CI 4.9 8.3) in the control arm.

indication.text: Treatment of adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).

citations.quote: BESPONSA is indicated for the treatment of adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).

target_moa.text: CD22-directed antibody-drug conjugate; a humanized IgG4 anti-CD22 antibody conjugated to N-acetyl-gamma-calicheamicin. Binding to CD22 leads to internalization and delivery of the cytotoxic calicheamicin payload, causing double-strand DNA breaks, apoptosis and cell death.

citations.quote: Inotuzumab ozogamicin is a CD22 targeted antibody-drug conjugate comprised of a humanized immunoglobulin IgG4 covalently attached via a linker to the small molecule, N-acetyl-gamma-calicheamicin.
The anticancer activity of inotuzumab ozogamicin is due to the binding of the ADC to CD22 expressing cells, followed by internalization of the ADC-C
the cytotoxic calicheamicin payload in a CD22-directed manner causing apoptosis and cell death.

**Mechanism of Action:** inotuzumab ozogamicin consists of a humanized IgG4 monoclonal antibody targeting CD22+ B-cells and N-acetyl-\gamma-calicheamicin, which induces DNA double-strand breaks resulting in cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.
Inotuzumab ozogamicin is a CD22 targeted antibody-drug conjugate comprised of a humanized immunoglobulin IgG4 covalently attached via a linker to the small molecule, N-acetyl-gamma-calicheamicin.

key_safety.text: Most common (>=20%) adverse reactions: thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, infection, anemia, leukopenia, fatigue, hemorrhage, pyrexia, nausea, headache, febrile neutropenia, transaminases increased, abdominal pain, gamma-glutamyltransferase increased, and hyperbilirubinemia. Most frequent serious AE was VOD (13%, 22/164). Infections occurred in 79/164 (48%) and hemorrhagic events in 54/164 (33%).

citations.quote: The most common (\ge 20\%) adverse reactions are thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, infection, anemia, leukopenia, fatigue, hemorrhage, pyrexia, nausea, headache, febrile neutropenia, transaminases increased, abdominal pain, gamma-glutamyltransferase increased, and hyperbilirubinemia. (6.1)
The most frequent serious adverse event in the inotuzumab ozogamicin arm was VOD (13%, 22/164) compared to investigator's choice of chemotherapy arm (<1%, 1/143).
Infections, including serious infections, some of which were life-threatening or fatal, were reported in 79/164 patients (48%).
Hemorrhagic events were reported in 54/164 patients (33%).

requirement.text: PMR 3259-1: Characterize toxicity after HSCT (including hepatic VOD, transplant-related [non-relapse] mortality, and non-transplant-related mortality) in adult and pediatric patients via analysis of registry data through at least day 180 post-transplantation, minimum duration no less than five years.

citations.quote: PMR 3259-1 Characterize toxicity after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) in adult and pediatric patients who receive inotuzumab ozogamicin. Include hepatic veno-occlusive disease, transplant related mortality (non-relapse mortality), and non-transplant related mortality. Conduct an analysis of registry data (for example the Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplantation Research registry) to evaluate safety at least through day 180 after transplantation. The number of available patients in the database will determine the sample size. Include details of all prior therapies. The minimum duration of the study is to be no less than five years.

requirement.text: PMR 3259-2: Conduct a randomized trial of at least 2 dose levels of inotuzumab ozogamicin in R/R ALL patients who are potential HSCT candidates at high risk for VOD, assessing hepatic VOD, transplant-related and non-transplant-related mortality, and efficacy including MRD-negativity.

citations.quote: PMR 3259-2 Conduct a randomized trial of at least 2 dose levels of inotuzumab ozogamicin in patients with relapsed or refractory acute lymphoblastic leukemia who are potential candidates for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and at high risk for developing veno-occlusive disease (VOD).

summary.text: BESPONSA received full (regular) approval on August 17, 2017 for adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor ALL. It had Breakthrough Therapy Designation (granted October 15, 2015), Orphan Drug Designation (granted March 25, 2013), and Priority Review; the BLA was submitted via rolling submission. It was not taken to advisory committee.

The benefit-risk assessment supports full approval of inotuzumab ozogamicin for the treatment of adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).
The FDA granted Breakthrough Therapy Designation to inotuzumab ozogamicin for the treatment of relapsed or refractory B-cell ALL on October 15, 2015.
Mar 25, 2013	FDA grants Orphan Drug Designation for inotuzumab ozogamicin for the treatment of precursor B-cell ALL.
The Applicant requested priority review with the submission of the final portion of the BLA, and the FDA granted priority review of the application.
The Applicant was granted rolling submission of the BLA on December 29, 2015.

description.text: Added treatment of relapsed or refractory CD22-positive B-cell precursor ALL in pediatric patients 1 year and older

citations.quote: This Prior Approval supplemental biologics license application provides for the treatment of relapsed or refractory CD22-positive B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in pediatric patients 1 year and older. In addition, this supplemental biologics license application provides for updates to Section 1 (Indications and Usage), Section 8.4 (Pediatric Use), Section 12.3 (Pharmacokinetics/Pediatric Patients), the addition of Section 12.6 (Immunogenicity) along with other relevant sections and editorial changes throughout the United States Prescribing Information (USPI). These changes are based on data from two studies: Study ITCC-059 (WI203581) "A Phase 1/2, multicenter, European, multi-cohort, open-label study in pediatric patients (\ge 1 and <18 years of age) with R/R CD22-positive ALL", as of the study PCD on 12 September 2022 and INO-Ped-ALL-1 (WI235086) "An open-label, multi-center Phase 1 study to assess safety and tolerability of InO in Japanese pediatric patients with R/R CD22-positive AL".
